conversation.content:
Hello there—I’m so glad you’re here. My name is Dr. Morales, and I’m the perinatal mental-health clinician who works alongside your OB team. I specialize in the emotional changes that can come with new motherhood, and today I’d like to spend a few quiet minutes doing a routine check-in with the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**—usually just called the **EPDS**.  

The EPDS is a short, 10-question survey that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling in the past seven days. It isn’t a test of your parenting—just a way to see how we can best support you. Everything you share stays confidential within your medical team, and this is a judgment-free space; there are no right or wrong answers, only your honest experience.  

We’ll go through one question at a time. I’ll ask each in everyday language, and you can answer however feels most comfortable. If anything feels confusing, just let me know and we’ll pause. Ready to begin?

**Question 1:** Over the past seven days, how often have you felt able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly? Not very often. I used to laugh all the time—my husband and I would crack each other up over the dumbest memes—but lately it feels like the baby monitor is the only sound in the house. I might smile once or twice if someone sends me a cute video, but it fades fast. I’d say I’ve only really laughed maybe once in the past week, and even that felt forced.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not really. I can’t remember the last time something actually felt funny enough to laugh out loud. It’s like I’m too tired or too worried to find anything amusing.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not much. I used to get excited about little stuff—like my favorite show dropping a new episode or even just a quiet cup of coffee—but now it all feels flat. I’ll think “I should be looking forward to this,” but the feeling never really shows up. Maybe once or twice I’ve felt a tiny spark, but it fades before I can grab onto it.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… pretty much every day. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s because I’m not doing something right—maybe my milk isn’t enough or I missed his sleepy cue. Yesterday I spilled a little pumped milk and I sat on the kitchen floor crying, telling myself I’m a terrible mom for wasting it. I know logically it’s just an accident, but the guilt still lands on me hard.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yeah, most days. I’ll be rocking the baby and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure he’s stopped breathing—even though he’s right there in my arms. Or I’ll lie awake picturing him choking in the crib even though the monitor’s on and he’s fine. There’s no real reason, but the worry just barges in and parks itself.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A few times. It’s like a sudden wave—my chest gets tight, I feel shaky, and I’m sure something awful is about to happen, even though nothing’s going on. Last night I was folding laundry and out of nowhere I had to sit down because I felt like I couldn’t breathe. It passed after a minute, but it left me rattled.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes, quite a lot. Between the night feedings, the constant worry that I’m not doing enough, and the pile of laundry that never shrinks, it feels like I’m drowning in small stuff. Some mornings I just stare at the mess and think, “I can’t do this today,” even though I still manage to push through. I keep telling myself I should be able to handle it, but it feels heavy almost every day.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah, that’s been happening. I’ll finally get the baby down, but then I lie there with my mind racing—going over everything I think I messed up or imagining terrible “what-ifs.” Even when I’m exhausted, it takes me forever to fall asleep, and when I do drift off, any little sound jolts me awake. I’d say it’s been like that at least four nights this week.
I have felt sad or miserable

Most of the time. It’s like a gray cloud that just hangs there. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly feel tears sliding down my face for no clear reason. Yesterday I looked out the window at the sunshine and felt nothing but heavy and empty. I’d say I’ve felt sad or miserable more days than not this past week.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s been like that several times this week. Sometimes it’s triggered—like when I couldn’t get the baby to latch and felt useless—but other times the tears just show up while I’m folding onesies or warming a bottle. I’ll catch myself sobbing in the kitchen and think, “I shouldn’t be this upset,” but I can’t stop it.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… that hasn’t crossed my mind. I feel overwhelmed and low, but I haven’t had any thoughts like that.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 23: Postpartum Depression/Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: __________

Presenting symptoms endorsed:
- Marked anhedonia (Q1, Q2)  
- Daily excessive guilt/self-blame regarding parenting (Q3)  
- Persistent, unexplained anxiety, catastrophic worries about infant safety (Q4)  
- Multiple sudden panic-like episodes (Q5)  
- Overwhelm and sense of inability to cope with routine tasks (Q6)  
- Mood-congruent insomnia (Q7)  
- Near-daily sad or empty mood and frequent crying spells (Q8, Q9)  

Pattern: Symptoms cluster in depressive and anxiety domains, present most days over the past week, and exceed typical postpartum adjustment.

Risk factors identified:
✓ Loss of pleasure and low mood  
✓ Sleep disruption related to rumination/guilt  
✓ Excessive guilt/worthlessness  
✓ Recurrent panic symptoms  
✓ Feeling "drowned" by daily demands  

Safety: Denies self-harm ideation (Q10); no suicidal intent or plan reported.

Screening impression: High clinical concern for postpartum major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety features; scores warrant prompt referral for comprehensive evaluation and possible treatment planning.
